chats.answer:
For running a pellet stove during a power outage, the power station with the largest usable battery capacity (Wh) will generally run it the longest.

My recommendation is to look at expandable LiFePO₄ power stations from EcoFlow, Bluetti, and Anker rather than small portable models.

Most pellet stoves consume approximately:

100–200 watts while operating normally.

300–600+ watts briefly during ignition, depending on the stove.

More power if the stove has additional fans or other electrical components.

For comparison, I'll use a pellet stove averaging 150 watts, with an estimated 85% battery-to-AC efficiency. Actual runtime will depend on your stove and how frequently it ignites.

chats.answer:
For running a pellet stove during a power outage, the power station with the largest usable battery capacity (Wh) will generally run it the longest, provided it can handle the stove's startup surge.

My recommendation is to look at large, expandable power stations from EcoFlow, Anker SOLIX, Bluetti, and Jackery.

Most pellet stoves use approximately:

Startup: 300–600 watts, sometimes more during ignition.

Normal operation: 60–150 watts, depending on the stove and fan settings.

Shutdown: Additional power for the exhaust fan to complete a safe shutdown.

For backup heating, I would prioritize battery capacity, pure sine wave AC output, and reliable power transfer over maximum advertised inverter wattage.

One question that will change my recommendation

What brand and model is your pellet stove? For example, Harman P43, Quadra-Fire, ComfortBilt HP22, or Englander.

With that information, I can compare power stations by estimated hours of heating and cost, rather than just battery size.
